Senator Grohoski, Representative Cloutier, and members of the Joint Standing Committee on
Taxation. My name is Garrett Mason. l am a resident of Lisbon Falls and a partner at Dirigo Public Affairs. l am here on behalf of the Portland Sea Dogs to respectfully oppose LD 1857,
specifically the provisions that repeal the qualified professional baseball facility tax credit enacted by the previous Legislature.
The Sea Dogs are proud to be Maine's home team, not just in name, but in unwavering
commitment to our state, our fans, and our community. We are particularly proud to contribute
tens of thousands of dollars each year to organizations that support Maine veterans, including
Honor Flight Maine and Wreaths Across America. We strongly support the expansion of
veterans' property tax exemptions included in Part A of this bill, but that support should not
come at the expense of targeted economic development tools that have helped institutions like
ours remain competitive and committed to Maine.
The Portland Sea Dogs made substantial business decisions based on the professional baseball facility tax credit passed with bipartisan support in the last legislative session. LD 2258 from the 131st Legislature stood on its own merits, achieved bipartisan enactment in both houses, and was signed by the Governor. That credit was not a giveaway; it was an incentive
designed to recognize the public and economic value that a professional team brings to Maine's largest city and the surrounding region. Thousands of Maine families, tourists, and local businesses benefit directly and indirectly from our games and community events.
Repealing the tax creditjust one year after its enactment sends a message that Maine is not a reliable partner. It penalizes those who acted in good faith and discourages future investment in economic and cultural infrastructure. If Maine wants to continue attracting and retaining assets
like the Sea Dogs, then we must maintain a stable and predictable policy environment.
For these reasons, we urge the Committee to reject Part B of LD 1857. Let's keep our commitments, support our veterans, and protect the economic engines that help make Maine a
great place to live, work, and play.
Thank you for your time and consideration.

Testimony of the Maine Municipal Association
In Opposition to Part A of LD 1857, An Act to Expand Property Tax Relief for Veterans and Their Survivors and to Modify
Certain Corporate Tax Expenditures
May 6, 2025
Senator Grohoski, Representative Cloutier and members of the Taxation Committee, my name is Kate Dufour, and I am submitting testimony in opposition to Part A of LD 1857 on behalf of MMA's Legislative Policy Committee, which establishes the association's positions on all municipally relevant legislation.
While municipal officials greatly appreciate the contributions of veterans of the U.S. Armed Forces, the approach envisioned in LD 1857 provides only one category of homeowners any relief. While there are veterans who undoubtedly need assistance in paying property taxes, there are young families, seniors and life-long volunteers who also need relief. Furthermore, absent full state reimbursement for lost property tax revenues, those costs are not only shifted to others in the community, but also onto the intended beneficiaries.
Instead, municipal leaders urge the committee to relieve the pressures placed on all property taxpayers.
Thank you for your time and consideration of the municipal perspective on this issue.

TESTIMONY OF MICHAEL J. ALLEN, ASSOCIATE COMMISSIONER FOR TAX POLICY
DEPARTMENT OF ADMINISTRATIVE AND FINANCIAL SERVICES
Before the Joint Standing Committee on Taxation Hearing Date: May 6, 2025
LD 1857 - "An Act to Expand Property Tax Relief for Veterans and Their Survivors and to Modify Certain Corporate Tax Expenditures"
Senator Grohoski, Representative Cloutier, and members of the Taxation Committee - good afternoon, my name is Michael Allen, Associate Commissioner for Tax Policy in the Department of Administrative and Financial Services. I am testifying at the request of the Administration Against LD 1857, "An Act to Expand Property Tax Relief for Veterans and Their Survivors and to Modify Certain Corporate Tax Expenditures."
Part A of the bill changes the property tax benefits for military veterans beginning with property tax years beginning on or after April 1, 2026. These changes are identical to those in LD 888 and similar to others this Committee has considered both this Session and last Session. The Administration testified in support of LD 888 and this Committee voted Ought To Pass As Amended.
Part B of the bill eliminates tax credits for investment in qualified professional baseball facilities and for major business headquarters expansion, eliminates the discounted rate on cigarette stamps for licensed distributors, eliminates the refund on sales tax on purchases of parts and supplies for windjammers, and reduces the value of the aggregate amount of tax credit certificates that the Finance Authority of Maine may authorize under the Maine Seed Capital Tax Credit Program for investments made in calendar year 2026 from $15,000,000 to $10,000,000.
1

The Administration opposes the changes made by Part B. The elimination of each of these programs raises its own policy and technical issues that should be given due consideration. In addition, adequate time should be given for the public and affected taxpayers to consider and respond to the Legislation. The accelerated timeline for this bill's public hearing is a cause for concern in itself and leaves little room for public participation.
Turning to technical concerns, the bill should be amended to clarify the tax year in which the credits under Title 36 are repealed and the eligibility for credits for projects in progress that have already been certified. At this time, only a preliminary review of the bill has been completed and there may be other technical issues.
The Administration looks forward to working with the Committee on the bill; representatives from MRS will be here for the Work Session to provide additional information and respond in detail to the Committee's questions.

Senator Grohoski, Representative Cloutier and colleagues on the Taxation Committee,
My name is Mike Tipping. I represent Senate District 8 in Penobscot County and I'm proud to present LD 1857, An Act to Expand Property Tax Relief for Veterans and Their Survivors
and to Modify Certain Corporate Tax Expenditures.
Maine has the fourth highest percentage of our population that has served in the armed forces of any state in the country. Most Maine veterans are older, with the largest group having served during the Vietnam era. One third have a disability.
High and rising property taxes hit some veterans especially hard, leading to the awful prospect of
older Mainers who have served our country losing their home and losing their independence.
That's why this committee has acted, passing property tax relief for veterans time and time
again. We passed a unanimous bill during the last legislature and we did so again earlier this
year.
We all feel good about those votes and the bills sail through the House and Senate -- no one
wants to vote against veterans -- but they don't go into effect, because they aren't funded.
This bill is different from the previous bills we've heard on this issue. In addition to the language
on veteran property tax relief, it also repeals or pares back a set of corporate-focused tax expenditures that are unneeded or undeiperforming. It allows us to better prioritize the tax
incentives under our purview as a committee and make sure the things we most care about are
given precedence.
Part B of this bill would eliminate some current tax expenditures, including:
The credit for professional baseball facilities we passed last year as a corporate handout to a single private equity firm that owns a baseball team in Portland.
The major business headquarters expansion credit, which only affects businesses with more than 5,000 employees and is duplicative of other credits already in Maine law.
The discounted rate on cigarette stamps for licensed distributors, a state subsidy on bulk purchases of cigarettes.

Senator Grohoski, Representative Cloutier, and distinguished members of the Joint Standing Committee on
Taxation, my name is Nate Cloutier, and I am here today on behalf of HospitaLityMaine, representing Maine's
restaurant and lodging industries. I am also testifying on behalf of the Maine Tourism Association (MTA). MTA
has been promoting Maine and supporting tourism-related businesses----from lodging and dining to camps, retail, guides, amusements, and historic attractions---for over 100 years. Hospita1ityMaine and the Maine Tourism
Association oppose LD 1857, "An Act to Expand Property Tax Relief for Veterans and Their Survivors and to
Modify Certain Corporate Tax Expenditures.
Our testimony concems Part B of LD 1857, which would eliminate tax credits for investment in qualified
professional baseball facilities and for major business headquarters expansion; reduce by $5 million the credit
authority under the Maine Seed Capital Tax Credit Program for CY 26 investments; and eliminate other discounts
and refunds.
Just one year ago, LD 2258, sponsored by Senate President Troy Jackson, was passed by the 131" Legislature
and signed into law by Governor Mills. The bill created a targeted tax credit to help the Portland Sea Dogs make
critical upgrades to the city-owned Hadlock Field, which included making the stadium ADA compliant. This investment is intended to help the team retain its MLB affiliation and ensure that Mainers and visitors with
disabilities can enjoy our local baseball experience.
There are significant benefits associated with having a Minor League Baseball (MiLB) team within our great
state. As we deliberate on various matters impacting our community, it's imperative to recognize the positive
contributions that minor league baseball makes to our economy, community spirit, and overall quality of life.
Economic Impact:
l. Job Creation: Minor league baseball teams are substantial job generators. From front office staff and
player personnel to game-day operations and facility maintenance, the presence of a MiLB team fosters
employment opportunities for a diverse range of individuals within our state.

2. Local Businesses: The influx of spectators attending minor league baseball games stimulates local businesses, including restaurants, hotels, and shops. This increased economic activity not only benefits the immediate vicinity of the ballpark but also ripples through neighboring communities.
3. Tourism Boost: Minor league baseball draws visitors from both within and outside the state. Families often plan vacations around attending games, contributing to tourism revenue and bolstering our state's reputation as a welcoming and vibrant destination.
Community Engagement:
1. Family-Friendly Entertainment: Minor league baseball offers affordable, family-friendly
entertaimnent. By providing an accessible and enjoyable experience, it promotes bonding within
families and strengthens the fabric of our communities.
2. Youth Development Programs: Many minor league teams actively engage with local youth through
community outreach programs, school partnerships, and youth clinics. These initiatives foster a sense of community pride, inspire the next generation of athletes, and contribute to the holistic development of
our youth.
3. Charitable Giving: The Sea Dogs have exemplified what it means to be a community partner with their charitable giving and fundraising efforts. Most notably the work they do With the Barbara Bush Children's Hospital and the Strike Out Cancer in Kids program. Raising over $5 million.
Quality of Life:
l. Civic Pride and Identity: Minor league baseball teams often become a source of civic pride and identity for communities. The team's success and affiliation with our state instill a sense of unity and belonging among residents. The Sea Dogs may have Portland in their name, but the reality is they are Maine's team.
2. Community Gathering: Baseball games serve as a gathering place for people of all ages and
backgrounds. The ballpark has become a venue for community events, charity drives, and social
activities, enhancing the social cohesion within our state.
Reneging on and repealing this credit would signal to the Sea Dogs, and to every existing Maine business and prospective investor, that our state's business environment is unpredictable and unstable. If the Sea Dogs are
planning or already undertaking infrastructure projects, what message would this send? We need to broadcast that
Maine is a stable, welcoming place to do business. It is far more expensive, time consuming, and risky to replace a lost asset than it is to maintain the one you already have.
Reversing course now would risk losing a cherished team like the Sea Dogs to New Hampshire or another state,
and with them, local jobs and economic activity that benefit our communities.
In conclusion, supporting minor league baseball teams in our state is not only an investment in our economy but also an investment in the well-being and vibrancy of our communities. The Sea Dogs have shown their dedication and commitment to their local communities and Maine as a whole. The committee should consider the far-
reaching benefits of these teams and explore opportunities to further strengthen their presence in Maine. We urge you to vote LD 1857 ought not to pass. Thank you for your time and attention. I would be happy to answer any
questions.
10050477:
Testimony by William Norbert Governmental Affairs and Communications Manager
In Opposition to a Portion of Part B of L.D. 1857
An Act to Expand Property Tax Relief for Veterans and Their Survivors and to Modify Certain Corporate Tax Expenditures
May 6, 2025
Joint Standing Committee on Taxation
Senator Grohoski, Representative Cloutier, and Distinguished Members of the Joint Standing Committee on Taxation:
My name is Bill Norbert. I am the Governmental Affairs and Communications Manager at the Finance Authority of Maine (FAME) and am testifying today in opposition to a portion of Part B of L.D. 1699, An Act to Create a Refundable Tax Credit for Agricultural Enterprises. We take no position on the other portions of the bill.
Part B of this bill would, among other things, reduce the value of the aggregate amount of tax credit certificates that FAME may authorize under the Maine Seed Capital Tax Credit Program for investments made in Calendar Year 2026 from $15 million to $10 million.
FAME has administered the Seed Capital Tax Credit Program since its creation by the Legislature in 1987-88. The credit is designed to encourage equity and near-equity investments in eligible Maine businesses, directly and through private venture capital funds. FAME may authorize state income tax credits or re-fundable tax credits to investors for 40 percent of the cash equity they provide to eligible Maine businesses. Investments may be used for fixed assets, research or working capital. Some of the Maine companies that have benefitted from the program include TimberHP in Madison; Tanbark Molded Fiber Products in Saco; Vertical Harvest in Westbrook; MedRhythms in Portland; bluShift Aerospace in Brunswick; Pumpspotting in Kittery; and Quoddy in Lewiston.
The Maine Economic Development Strategy 2020-2029: A Focus on Talent and Innovation ("Strategic Plan") issued by the Department of Economic and Community Development (DECD) referenced the Seed Capital Tax Credit Program as a tool to help promote innovation in the state. The Strategic Plan included a proposed action to increase
1

the annual program cap from $5 million to $15 million in order to assist startups and create new jobs in Maine.
As you may recall from your recent consideration of L.D. 125, An Act to Increase the Total Amount of Credits Authorized Under the Maine Seed Capital Tax Credit Program, the current annual aggregate tax credit certificate program limit of $15 million is scheduled to decrease to $5 million in 2027. Although it is difficult to predict with complete certainty, we expect significant interest and activity in the program in 2026 since businesses, investors, venture funds, and others realize it will be the final year (at least for now) for the $15 million limit in allowable credits. We hope you will resist this effort to lower the maximum limit during the final year of the program's heightened credit level, regardless of the good intentions behind this bill--providing more property tax relief to our veterans and their survivors.
Thank you for your consideration of my comments and I would be happy to answer any questions.
2
